blocks.text: The first two visions portray devastation by locusts and fire, but Amos responds by pleading for “Jacob,” described as small. In both cases the threatened judgment does not proceed. The third vision marks a change: the Lord declares that he will no longer pass by Israel. The object traditionally called a plumb-line rests on a rare term whose meaning remains uncertain; “plumb-line” is an influential interpretation, but the passage should not be made to carry elaborate measurement symbolism with more confidence than the wording allows.

The scene at Bethel has several distinct voices that should not be blended together. Amaziah reports Amos to the king and then commands Amos to leave and cease prophesying there; Amos replies by describing his own call from tending flocks and sycamore trees; only then comes the judgment speech. Amos’s statement that he was not a prophet or a prophet’s son may refer to professional status, present identity, or connection with a prophetic guild. It should not be used as a simple rejection of learning, paid ministry, or every religious institution.

The opening visions show prophetic authority as including advocacy for a threatened people, not only denunciation. At the same time, the chapter’s judgments of exile and violence call for lament and ethical scrutiny; they do not authorize readers to carry out vengeance, coercion, war, or punishment in the prophet’s name.
